newsitem.title: USA: Wis., Mich. officials detail welfare reform impact.
newsitem.headline: Wis., Mich. officials detail welfare reform impact.

text.p: Welfare reform is working in Michigan and Wisconsin, saving those states millions of dollars, two state officials said Thursday.

Speaking at a Chicago Municipal Analysts Society meeting here, Paul Reinhart, director of Michigan's office of health and human services, said reform efforts since 1991 have cut Michigan caseloads to 165,000 from 227,000 and costs to government to $775 million from $1.3 billion a year.
"It's fair to conclude reform policies have had an impact, more than you would expect from the strong economy which Michigan has now," Reinhart said.
In Wisconsin, meanwhile, Robin Gates, acting deputy secretary of department of work force development, reported that case loads also dropped significantly in that state.
However, he cautioned that other costs have risen. For example, in day care the state is projecting it will have to more than double expenditures over the next two years.
Michigan saw Medicaid expenditures rising to $4.8 billion in the current fiscal year from $3.2 billion in fiscal 1991 as more children were covered, according to Reinhart.
Michigan and Wisconsin both emphasised job placement in their reform, according to the state officials.
In Wisconsin, a shortage of labour has proved to be a plus for the state's welfare reform efforts, Gates said.
"Labor market economists are telling us we're still likely to see a tight labour market," he said. "It's perfect for welfare reform."

With declining caseloads, both states anticipate seeing surpluses as a result of federal block grants for welfare that are based on 1994 caseloads or an average of caseloads from 1992 to 1994, whichever is greater.
Michigan is projecting a welfare funding balance of $220 million for fiscal 1998, which Reinhart said would provide a cushion for the state in the event of an economic downturn.
But Joe O'Keefe, a director at Standard & Poor's Corp, said while states are currently fiscally strong, their present financial cushions are inadequate.

He warned that pressures from welfare spending could result in cutbacks in other state funding programmes, such as for education. He added, however, that the federal government would be unlikely to let states and their local governments suffer as a result of welfare reform.
